TITLE: CoWoS Explained: Advanced Chip Packaging and the Real Bottleneck Behind AI GPUs
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: Why does AI chip supply depend on packaging? An in-depth guide to TSMC's CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate), silicon interposers, HBM integration, CoWoS-S vs CoWoS-L vs CoWoS-R, chiplets, the reticle limit, competing technologies like Intel EMIB and Foveros, and what comes next.

content:
Short answer

CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) is TSMC's advanced packaging technology that places a GPU or accelerator die side by side with stacks of HBM memory on a silicon interposer, connecting them with thousands of ultra-fine wires. It is what lets chips like NVIDIA's H100, H200 and B200 and AMD's Instinct MI300X reach several terabytes per second of memory bandwidth. Because nearly every leading AI accelerator needs it, CoWoS capacity became a major bottleneck for AI chip supply from 2023 onwards, alongside HBM production itself.

Why packaging suddenly matters

For decades, chip progress came mainly from shrinking transistors. AI accelerators now hit two walls that transistor shrinking alone cannot fix:

1. The memory wall: AI workloads need far more memory bandwidth than traditional circuit-board memory can deliver. The answer is HBM: DRAM dies stacked vertically and placed millimetres from the processor with a very wide interface (1,024 bits per stack for HBM3/HBM3E, 2,048 for HBM4). 2. The reticle limit: lithography machines can only expose an area of about 26 × 33 mm (around 858 mm²) in one shot, which caps the size of a single die. The largest AI chips are already at that limit.

Advanced packaging solves both by joining multiple dies, logic and memory, into one package that behaves like a single, giant chip.

How CoWoS works

The name describes the layers from top to bottom:

1. Chip: the logic die (GPU) and HBM stacks. 2. on Wafer: these sit on a silicon interposer, a thin piece of silicon with very dense wiring layers (redistribution layers) and through-silicon vias (TSVs). The interposer is made on a wafer, hence the name. 3. on Substrate: the interposer is mounted on an organic package substrate that connects to the circuit board.

The interposer's wiring is much finer than any circuit board, allowing thousands of connections between the GPU and each HBM stack at high speed and low power. That is how an H100 reaches about 3.35 TB/s and a B200 about 8 TB/s.

CoWoS variants

Why Blackwell needed CoWoS-L

NVIDIA's Blackwell B200 joins two reticle-sized GPU dies with a 10 TB/s die-to-die link and eight HBM3E stacks in a single package. A full silicon interposer that large is impractical, so CoWoS-L uses small silicon bridges embedded in a larger organic interposer to link the dies and memory where dense wiring is needed. The two dies then appear to software as one GPU. See B200 vs H100 and GB200 NVL72 explained.

Why CoWoS became a bottleneck

  • Demand exploded: the AI boom from 2023 sent orders for H100-class GPUs far beyond plans.
  • Long lead times: building packaging lines takes many months, with specialised equipment.
  • Complexity and yield: combining several expensive dies means one defect can waste the whole package, so testing before assembly ("known good die") is critical.
  • Coupled supply: each package also needs HBM stacks from SK hynix, Samsung or Micron, which were in short supply too.

TSMC expanded CoWoS capacity aggressively, and outsourced assembly and test companies (OSATs) such as ASE and Amkor added capacity for parts of the process. Packaging and test constraints have also rippled into supply of ordinary chips, as covered in our report on the 2026 chip shortage.

Other advanced packaging technologies

AMD's Instinct MI300X is a striking example: eight compute chiplets stacked on four I/O dies, combined with eight HBM3 stacks for 192 GB of memory, using both 3D stacking and 2.5D packaging. See MI355X vs B200.

2.5D vs 3D packaging

  • 2.5D: dies sit side by side on an interposer (CoWoS, EMIB). Easier thermal management; limited by interposer area.
  • 3D: dies stacked on top of each other (HBM itself, SoIC, Foveros). Shortest connections and highest density, but harder to cool and test.

Future AI chips combine both: 3D-stacked logic and memory placed on large 2.5D interposers.

What comes next

  • Bigger interposers: packages spanning several reticle sizes with more HBM stacks, for example in NVIDIA's Rubin generation and beyond.
  • HBM4 and custom base dies: HBM4 doubles the interface width, and its base die can be customised and made on logic processes, blurring memory and compute.
  • Co-packaged optics: placing optical connections inside the package to move data between chips with less power.
  • Panel-level packaging: using large rectangular panels instead of round wafers to make bigger interposers more efficiently.
  • Glass substrates: flatter, more stable substrates for very large packages.
  • Wafer-scale integration: the extreme approach taken by Cerebras, building a whole wafer as one chip. See Cerebras WSE-3.

Why this matters for GPU buyers and renters

Packaging and HBM capacity, not just chip fabrication, determine how many data center GPUs can be built. That shapes availability and pricing for H100, H200 and B200 GPUs in the cloud; follow daily rates in our GPU cloud price tracker and read why GPU prices are rising.

Frequently asked questions

What does CoWoS stand for?

Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate: chips are mounted on a silicon interposer (made on a wafer), which is then mounted on a package substrate.

Do consumer GPUs use CoWoS?

Generally no. Consumer graphics cards use GDDR memory on the circuit board, which does not need an interposer. CoWoS is used for HBM-based data center accelerators.

Is CoWoS only made by TSMC?

CoWoS is TSMC's brand. Other companies offer comparable 2.5D packaging, such as Intel's EMIB and Samsung's I-Cube, and OSATs handle some steps of the process.

Why not just make one bigger chip?

The reticle limit caps single-die size, and very large dies have low yields because one defect can ruin the whole die. Splitting a design into chiplets and packaging them together is cheaper and scales further.

TITLE: Data, Tensor, Pipeline and Expert Parallelism Explained: How LLMs Train on Thousands of GPUs
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
IMG: How LLMs Train on Thousands of GPUs
EXCERPT: No single GPU can train a frontier model. An in-depth guide to data parallelism, ZeRO and FSDP, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, sequence and context parallelism and expert parallelism: how each splits the work, what it costs in communication, and how they combine into 3D and 4D parallelism.
KEY: Training a large language model requires splitting the work across many GPUs in several ways at once. Data parallelism gives each GPU a different slice of the batch; ZeRO/FSDP shards optimizer states, gradients and weights so they fit in memory; tensor parallelism splits individual matrix multiplications across GPUs; pipeline parallelism places different layers on different GPUs; context parallelism splits long sequences; and expert parallelism spreads mixture-of-experts layers. Frontier runs combine these into 3D or 4D parallelism. Meta, for example, trained Llama 3 405B on up to 16,000 H100 GPUs using tensor, context, pipeline and data parallelism together.
content:
Short answer

Training a large language model requires splitting the work across many GPUs in several ways at once. Data parallelism gives each GPU a different slice of the batch; ZeRO/FSDP shards optimizer states, gradients and weights so they fit in memory; tensor parallelism splits individual matrix multiplications across GPUs; pipeline parallelism places different layers on different GPUs; context parallelism splits long sequences; and expert parallelism spreads mixture-of-experts layers. Frontier runs combine these into 3D or 4D parallelism. Meta, for example, trained Llama 3 405B on up to 16,000 H100 GPUs using tensor, context, pipeline and data parallelism together.

Why one GPU is not enough

Two limits force parallelism:

1. Memory. Mixed-precision training with Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter for weights, gradients and optimizer states, before activations. A 70B model needs over 1.1 TB; an H100 has 80 GB. See AI training vs inference. 2. Time. Training compute is about 6 × parameters × tokens. Llama 3.1 405B needed roughly 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs; on one GPU that would take centuries. See LLM training cost.

The challenge is to split the work so that GPUs spend their time computing, not waiting for each other. Every strategy trades memory savings and speed against communication, which is why fast interconnects like NVLink and NVSwitch and InfiniBand or AI Ethernet matter so much.

1. Data parallelism (DP)

Every GPU holds a full copy of the model and processes a different mini-batch. After the backward pass, GPUs average their gradients with an all-reduce operation, so all copies stay identical.

  • Pros: simple, scales well, communication once per step.
  • Cons: each GPU must fit the whole model plus optimizer states, which is impossible for large models.
  • Communication: all-reduce of all gradients every step.

2. ZeRO and FSDP: sharded data parallelism

ZeRO (from Microsoft's DeepSpeed) removes data parallelism's memory redundancy by sharding state across the data-parallel GPUs:

With ZeRO-3, each GPU gathers the weights it needs for a layer just before using it, then discards them. PyTorch's Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) implements the same idea natively.

  • Pros: trains models far larger than one GPU's memory using only data-parallel logic.
  • Cons: more communication (all-gather weights, reduce-scatter gradients); works best with fast interconnects and large batches.

3. Tensor parallelism (TP)

Tensor parallelism splits individual layers. A large matrix multiplication is divided by columns or rows across GPUs, each computing part of the result. NVIDIA's Megatron-LM showed an efficient pattern for transformers: split the first MLP matrix by columns and the second by rows, so only one all-reduce is needed per MLP block; attention heads are split across GPUs the same way.

  • Pros: reduces memory for weights and activations per GPU; lowers latency per step.
  • Cons: communication inside every layer, multiple times per forward and backward pass.
  • Rule of thumb: keep tensor parallelism within a single NVLink domain, typically the 8 GPUs of one server or the 72 GPUs of a GB200 NVL72 rack, because it needs the highest bandwidth.

4. Pipeline parallelism (PP)

Pipeline parallelism assigns different layers to different GPUs: GPU 1 runs layers 1–20, GPU 2 runs 21–40, and so on. Activations flow forward through the stages and gradients flow back.

The problem is the pipeline bubble: while GPU 1 works on a batch, later GPUs wait. The fix is splitting each batch into many micro-batches so stages work on different micro-batches at once. Schedules such as GPipe, 1F1B (one forward, one backward) and interleaved schedules shrink the bubble further.

  • Pros: communication only between neighbouring stages, so it works across slower links between servers.
  • Cons: bubbles waste compute; balancing layers across stages is fiddly; more micro-batches need more activation memory.

5. Sequence and context parallelism

Long sequences create huge activation memory, and attention cost grows with the square of sequence length. Sequence parallelism splits non-attention operations (such as layer norm and dropout) along the sequence dimension alongside tensor parallelism. Context parallelism goes further and splits the whole sequence across GPUs, using techniques like ring attention to pass keys and values between them. This is how models are trained with 128K-token and longer context windows.

6. Expert parallelism (EP)

In mixture-of-experts models, each MoE layer has many experts. Expert parallelism places different experts on different GPUs and routes each token to the GPUs holding its chosen experts using all-to-all communication. DeepSeek-V3, for example, spread its 256 routed experts across many GPUs.

  • Pros: lets models grow to hundreds of billions of parameters with modest compute per token.
  • Cons: all-to-all traffic is heavy and uneven; load balancing between experts is critical.

Putting it together: 3D and 4D parallelism

Real training runs combine strategies along different dimensions of the cluster:

Example: with 16,384 GPUs you might use tensor parallel 8 × pipeline parallel 16 × data parallel 128. Meta's Llama 3 paper describes exactly this kind of 4D parallelism (tensor, context, pipeline and data) to train the 405B model on up to 16,000 H100 GPUs.

Measuring efficiency

The key metric is model FLOPs utilization (MFU): the fraction of the GPUs' peak throughput spent on useful model maths. Large dense-model runs typically reach roughly 35–50% MFU; communication, pipeline bubbles, memory traffic and failures eat the rest. See MFU and GPU utilization explained.

Other techniques that save memory

  • Activation checkpointing (recomputation): discard some activations in the forward pass and recompute them during the backward pass, trading compute for memory.
  • Mixed precision and FP8 training: smaller numbers mean less memory and faster maths. See mixed precision training.
  • Offloading: move optimizer states to CPU memory or NVMe (slower, but helpful on small setups).
  • Gradient accumulation: simulate large batches on limited GPUs by summing gradients over several steps.

Frameworks

  • Megatron-LM / Megatron Core (NVIDIA): tensor, pipeline, sequence, context and expert parallelism for large-scale training.
  • DeepSpeed (Microsoft): ZeRO stages, pipeline parallelism and offloading.
  • PyTorch FSDP and TorchTitan: native sharding and composable parallelism.
  • JAX with XLA: used on TPUs and GPUs, with sharding annotations handled by the compiler.

Frequently asked questions

Which parallelism should I start with?

For fine-tuning on a few GPUs, start with FSDP or DeepSpeed ZeRO. Add tensor parallelism only when a single layer or the model's activations no longer fit, and keep it inside one server.

Why keep tensor parallelism within a server?

It communicates inside every layer, so it needs NVLink-class bandwidth (hundreds of GB/s to over 1 TB/s per GPU). Across a network it would leave GPUs waiting.

Is pipeline parallelism still used?

Yes, especially for very large models and clusters, because its point-to-point communication tolerates slower inter-node links. Better schedules have reduced the bubble problem.

Does inference use the same techniques?

Partly. Inference uses tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism to fit and speed up large models, but no gradients or optimizer states, so memory needs are much lower. See LLM inference engines compared.

Sources and further reading

  • Shoeybi et al., Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (2019)
  • Rajbhandari et al., ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (2019)
  • Huang et al., GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism (2018)
  • Narayanan et al., Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM (2021)
  • Meta, The Llama 3 Herd of Models (2024)
  • PyTorch, Fully Sharded Data Parallel

TITLE: Write Your First CUDA Kernel: A Beginner's Guide to GPU Programming (With Code)
LABEL: TUTORIAL
EXCERPT: A hands-on introduction to CUDA programming: write, compile and run your first GPU kernel, understand threads, blocks, grids and warps, use the grid-stride loop, measure performance, then learn about memory coalescing, shared memory, tensor cores and when to use Triton or cuBLAS instead.
KEY: CUDA lets you write C++ functions called kernels that run on thousands of GPU threads at once. You mark a function with __global__, launch it with the kernel<<<blocks, threads>>>(args) syntax, and each thread works out which piece of data to process from its block and thread index. This guide walks through a complete vector-add program, explains threads, blocks, grids and warps, and covers the performance ideas that matter most: memory coalescing, shared memory and occupancy, plus when to use libraries like cuBLAS or higher-level tools like Triton instead.
content:
Short answer

CUDA lets you write C++ functions called kernels that run on thousands of GPU threads at once. You mark a function with __global__, launch it with the kernel<<<blocks, threads>>>(args) syntax, and each thread works out which piece of data to process from its block and thread index. This guide walks through a complete vector-add program, explains threads, blocks, grids and warps, and covers the performance ideas that matter most: memory coalescing, shared memory and occupancy, plus when to use libraries like cuBLAS or higher-level tools like Triton instead.

What you need

  • An NVIDIA GPU (any recent GeForce, RTX or data center card)
  • The CUDA Toolkit from NVIDIA, which includes the nvcc compiler
  • A C++ compiler (Visual Studio on Windows, GCC on Linux)

No GPU? Rent one by the hour from a cloud provider; compare prices in our GPU cloud price tracker. For background, see What is CUDA? and How a GPU works.

The CUDA mental model

  • Host = the CPU and its memory. Device = the GPU and its memory.
  • A kernel is a function that runs on the device, executed by many threads in parallel.
  • Threads are grouped into blocks (up to 1,024 threads each), and blocks form a grid.
  • Each block runs on one streaming multiprocessor (SM); the hardware executes threads in groups of 32 called warps.
  • Every thread knows its position through built-in variables: threadIdx, blockIdx, blockDim and gridDim.

Your first kernel: adding two vectors

Save this as add.cu:

#include <cstdio>
#include <cmath>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// Runs on the GPU: each thread adds a subset of elements.
__global__ void add(int n, const float* x, const float* y, float* out) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;   // global thread index
    int stride = blockDim.x * gridDim.x;             // total threads in the grid
    for (; i < n; i += stride) {                      // grid-stride loop
        out[i] = x[i] + y[i];
    }
}

int main() {
    const int n = 1 << 24;                            // 16.7 million elements
    float *x, *y, *out;
    cudaMallocManaged(&x, n * sizeof(float));         // memory visible to CPU and GPU
    cudaMallocManaged(&y, n * sizeof(float));
    cudaMallocManaged(&out, n * sizeof(float));

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { x[i] = 1.0f; y[i] = 2.0f; }

    int threads = 256;
    int blocks = (n + threads - 1) / threads;
    add<<<blocks, threads>>>(n, x, y, out);
    cudaError_t err = cudaDeviceSynchronize();        // wait for the GPU to finish
    if (err != cudaSuccess) { printf("CUDA error: %s\n", cudaGetErrorString(err)); return 1; }

    float max_error = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) max_error = fmaxf(max_error, fabsf(out[i] - 3.0f));
    printf("Max error: %f\n", max_error);

    cudaFree(x); cudaFree(y); cudaFree(out);
    return 0;
}

Compile and run:

nvcc -O3 add.cu -o add
./add

You should see Max error: 0.000000.

What just happened

1. cudaMallocManaged allocated unified memory that both CPU and GPU can access; the driver moves data as needed. 2. add<<<blocks, threads>>> launched about 65,536 blocks of 256 threads, one thread per element. 3. Each thread computed its global index from blockIdx, blockDim and threadIdx. 4. The grid-stride loop means the kernel still works if you launch fewer threads than elements. 5. cudaDeviceSynchronize waited for the asynchronous kernel and reported any errors.

Explicit memory copies

Unified memory is convenient, but production code often manages transfers explicitly for predictable performance:

float *d_x;
cudaMalloc(&d_x, n * sizeof(float));
cudaMemcpy(d_x, h_x, n * sizeof(float), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);
// ... launch kernels using d_x ...
cudaMemcpy(h_x, d_x, n * sizeof(float), cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost);
cudaFree(d_x);

Moving data over PCIe is slow compared with GPU memory, so the golden rule is: copy data to the GPU once, do as much work there as possible, and copy results back once.

Measuring performance

Vector add does almost no maths per byte, so it is memory-bound: its speed is limited by memory bandwidth. Measure effective bandwidth with CUDA events:

cudaEvent_t start, stop;
cudaEventCreate(&start); cudaEventCreate(&stop);
cudaEventRecord(start);
add<<<blocks, threads>>>(n, x, y, out);
cudaEventRecord(stop);
cudaEventSynchronize(stop);
float ms = 0; cudaEventElapsedTime(&ms, start, stop);
double gbps = 3.0 * n * sizeof(float) / (ms / 1000.0) / 1e9;   // 2 reads + 1 write
printf("%.3f ms, %.1f GB/s\n", ms, gbps);

Run the kernel once to warm up (and to move unified memory to the GPU) before timing. A well-written memory-bound kernel reaches a large fraction of the GPU's rated bandwidth. For deeper analysis, use NVIDIA's profilers: Nsight Systems (nsys) for timelines and Nsight Compute (ncu) for kernel-level metrics. The roofline model simulator shows why some kernels are limited by bandwidth and others by compute.

The performance ideas that matter most

1. Memory coalescing

When the 32 threads of a warp access consecutive addresses, the hardware combines them into a few wide memory transactions. Scattered or strided access wastes bandwidth. Our kernel is coalesced because thread i reads element i.

2. Shared memory

Each SM has fast on-chip shared memory that threads in a block can use cooperatively. The classic use is tiling: load a tile of data from slow global memory once, then reuse it many times from shared memory. This is the core idea behind fast matrix multiplication and FlashAttention.

__global__ void tile_example(const float* in, float* out) {
    __shared__ float tile[256];
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    tile[threadIdx.x] = in[i];
    __syncthreads();                 // wait until the whole tile is loaded
    // ... threads can now read neighbours' values cheaply from tile[] ...
    out[i] = tile[threadIdx.x];
}

3. Occupancy and block size

Each SM can host a limited number of threads, registers and shared memory. Enough active warps let the GPU hide memory latency by switching between them. Block sizes of 128–512 threads (multiples of 32) are good starting points.

4. Avoid warp divergence

If threads in a warp take different branches of an if, the warp executes both paths one after another. Keep branches uniform within warps where possible.

5. Use the right precision and tensor cores

Most AI maths runs on tensor cores in FP16, BF16, FP8 or FP4, which are far faster than regular CUDA cores. Programming them directly (WMMA, MMA instructions, or CUTLASS) is advanced; most developers reach them through libraries. See tensor cores vs CUDA cores and precision formats.

Don't reinvent the wheel: libraries and higher-level tools

A hand-written naive matrix multiply is typically many times slower than cuBLAS. Write custom kernels when you need to fuse several operations to avoid memory round trips, or for operations no library provides.

A learning path

1. Vector add, then element-wise operations (ReLU, scaling). 2. Reductions (sum, max) using shared memory and warp shuffles. 3. Tiled matrix multiplication; compare with cuBLAS. 4. Softmax and layer norm kernels, the building blocks of transformers. 5. Try the same kernels in Triton and compare effort and speed. 6. Read about FlashAttention and how GPUs work at the hardware level.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to know C++ to use CUDA?

For CUDA C++, yes, basic C++ is enough to start. Alternatives include Triton and CuPy (Python), Numba (Python), and CUDA Python bindings.

Does CUDA work on AMD GPUs?

Not directly. AMD's ROCm platform offers HIP, a very similar programming model, and tools to convert CUDA code. See AMD vs NVIDIA for AI.

Why is my first kernel slower than the CPU?

Small problems, data transfer time and the first-launch overhead can outweigh GPU speed. GPUs shine on large, parallel workloads with data that stays on the device.

Should AI engineers learn CUDA?

You don't need it to train or use models, but understanding CUDA explains why techniques like FlashAttention, fused kernels and quantization make models faster, and it is valuable for performance engineering roles.

Sources and further reading

  • NVIDIA, CUDA C++ Programming Guide
  • NVIDIA, CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide
  • NVIDIA Developer Blog, An Even Easier Introduction to CUDA
  • OpenAI, Triton documentation
  • NVIDIA, CUTLASS on GitHub

TITLE: InfiniBand vs Ethernet for AI: RDMA, RoCE, Spectrum-X and Ultra Ethernet Explained
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: AI clusters live or die by their network. An in-depth comparison of InfiniBand and Ethernet for AI training and inference: RDMA and RoCE, scale-up vs scale-out, congestion control, NVIDIA Quantum and Spectrum-X, the Ultra Ethernet Consortium, topologies and how to choose.
KEY: Large AI clusters connect thousands of GPUs with a back-end network that must move huge volumes of data with very low latency and no packet loss. InfiniBand, now mainly supplied by NVIDIA, has long been the default for AI training thanks to native RDMA, credit-based lossless flow control and in-network computing. Ethernet has caught up through RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet), AI-tuned platforms like NVIDIA Spectrum-X and the open Ultra Ethernet standard. Both now run some of the world's largest clusters; Meta trained Llama 3 on two 24,000-GPU clusters, one using InfiniBand and one using RoCE Ethernet.
content:
Short answer

Large AI clusters connect thousands of GPUs with a back-end network that must move huge volumes of data with very low latency and no packet loss. InfiniBand, now mainly supplied by NVIDIA, has long been the default for AI training thanks to native RDMA, credit-based lossless flow control and in-network computing. Ethernet has caught up through RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet), AI-tuned platforms like NVIDIA Spectrum-X and the open Ultra Ethernet standard. Both now run some of the world's largest clusters; Meta trained Llama 3 on two 24,000-GPU clusters, one using InfiniBand and one using RoCE Ethernet.

Why the network matters so much for AI

When you train a model across many GPUs, they constantly exchange data: averaging gradients, gathering sharded weights, passing activations between pipeline stages, and routing tokens to experts in mixture-of-experts models. See distributed training and parallelism.

These are collective operations (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-to-all), and every GPU must wait for the slowest participant. A single congested link or dropped packet can stall thousands of GPUs worth millions of dollars. AI networking therefore cares about:

  • Bandwidth: typically 400 to 800 Gb/s per GPU today.
  • Tail latency: the slowest flows, not the average, decide step time.
  • Losslessness: retransmissions are expensive at this scale.
  • Scale: tens of thousands to over 100,000 GPUs.

Scale-up vs scale-out networks

Scale-up links are roughly 10 times faster than scale-out links, which is why bandwidth-hungry parallelism stays inside the NVLink domain; see NVLink and NVSwitch explained and GB200 NVL72. This article focuses on scale-out networking.

RDMA: the foundation

Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) lets one machine read or write another machine's memory directly, bypassing the operating system and CPU. With GPUDirect RDMA, the network card moves data straight to and from GPU memory. This cuts latency and frees CPUs. Both InfiniBand and modern AI Ethernet are built around RDMA; libraries such as NVIDIA's NCCL use it to run collectives across the cluster.

InfiniBand

InfiniBand was designed for high-performance computing and has native RDMA, credit-based flow control (a sender only transmits when the receiver has buffer space, so packets are not dropped), adaptive routing and centralised management through a subnet manager.

NVIDIA's InfiniBand platforms include Quantum-2 (400 Gb/s NDR) and Quantum-X800 (800 Gb/s XDR), with ConnectX network adapters. Its SHARP technology performs parts of reductions inside the switches, reducing traffic for all-reduce operations.

Strengths: mature, very low latency, predictable performance, excellent tooling for HPC and AI. Weaknesses: effectively one main vendor, specialised skills, often higher cost, separate from the Ethernet used elsewhere in the data center.

Ethernet for AI

Standard Ethernet is "best effort": switches drop packets when queues overflow. For AI, Ethernet adds:

  • RoCEv2: RDMA carried over UDP/IP so it can be routed across large networks.
  • Lossless or near-lossless behaviour: Priority Flow Control (PFC) and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) with congestion control algorithms such as DCQCN.
  • Advanced load balancing: packet spraying and adaptive routing spread traffic across all paths instead of pinning each flow to one.

NVIDIA Spectrum-X

An end-to-end Ethernet platform combining Spectrum switches with SuperNICs, adaptive routing, congestion control and telemetry tuned for AI collectives. NVIDIA positions it for very large AI factories that want Ethernet operations with InfiniBand-like performance.

Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC)

An industry group including AMD, Arista, Broadcom, Cisco, Intel, Meta, Microsoft and others, created to modernise Ethernet for AI and HPC. Its specification defines a new transport with multipath packet spraying, out-of-order delivery and modern congestion control, aiming to match InfiniBand's performance on open, multi-vendor hardware. UEC published its 1.0 specification in 2025.

Strengths of Ethernet: multi-vendor competition, huge ecosystem, familiar operations, scales to enormous sizes, one technology across the data center. Weaknesses: needs careful tuning (PFC storms, congestion), performance depends heavily on the switch and NIC features used.

InfiniBand vs Ethernet comparison

Topology: how the switches connect

  • Fat-tree / Clos: multiple tiers of switches give every server many equal paths with full bandwidth; the standard for AI.
  • Rail-optimised design: GPU 0 of every server connects to the same "rail" of switches, GPU 1 to another, and so on. Because collectives often communicate between same-numbered GPUs, most traffic stays within one switch hop.
  • Oversubscription: AI back-end networks are usually built non-blocking (1:1), unlike typical enterprise networks.
  • Optics: at 800G, optical transceivers become a significant share of cost and power. Co-packaged optics, which put optics next to the switch chip, are arriving to improve efficiency.

Inference networking

Inference is less network-intensive than training, but large MoE models spread across many GPUs, and disaggregated prefill/decode serving, increasingly need fast RDMA networks too. See LLM inference engines compared.

How to choose

  • Small to mid-size training clusters (up to a few thousand GPUs): InfiniBand is the simplest path to predictable performance.
  • Hyperscale clusters or mixed workloads: AI-tuned Ethernet offers vendor choice and operational consistency.
  • Cloud renters: check which interconnect a GPU cloud provides for multi-node jobs; it matters as much as the GPU model. Compare GPU prices in our GPU cloud price tracker and read What is a GPU cluster?.

Frequently asked questions

Is InfiniBand faster than Ethernet?

At the same link speed, raw bandwidth is similar. InfiniBand traditionally had lower and more predictable latency, while modern AI Ethernet platforms close much of the gap through better congestion control and load balancing.

What is RoCE?

RDMA over Converged Ethernet: a way to run RDMA on Ethernet networks. RoCEv2, which works over IP and can be routed, is the version used in AI clusters.

Does a single GPU server need InfiniBand?

No. Inside one server, GPUs talk over NVLink. Back-end networking only matters when a job spans multiple servers.

What does 800G mean?

800 gigabits per second per port, about 100 GB/s. AI clusters typically provide one such link per GPU.

TITLE: vLLM vs SGLang vs TensorRT-LLM vs llama.cpp vs Ollama: LLM Inference Engines Compared

EXCERPT: Which LLM inference engine should you use? An in-depth comparison of vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio and MLX: how PagedAttention, continuous batching and prefix caching work, hardware support, throughput vs latency, and which to pick for local use or production serving.
KEY: An LLM inference engine is the software that loads a model onto your hardware and turns prompts into tokens as efficiently as possible. For production serving on GPUs, the leading open-source choices are vLLM and SGLang (high throughput, many users), with NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM for maximum performance on NVIDIA hardware. For local and personal use, llama.cpp and the apps built on it, Ollama and LM Studio, run quantized models on almost any computer, and MLX is optimised for Apple Silicon. content:
Short answer

An LLM inference engine is the software that loads a model onto your hardware and turns prompts into tokens as efficiently as possible. For production serving on GPUs, the leading open-source choices are vLLM and SGLang (high throughput, many users), with NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM for maximum performance on NVIDIA hardware. For local and personal use, llama.cpp and the apps built on it, Ollama and LM Studio, run quantized models on almost any computer, and MLX is optimised for Apple Silicon. The right choice depends on whether you care most about throughput, latency, ease of use or hardware flexibility.

Why the engine matters

The same model on the same GPU can run several times faster or slower depending on the engine. Serving LLMs is hard because:

  • Decode is memory-bound: each token requires reading the full weights; see prefill vs decode.
  • The KV cache is large and grows unpredictably: every request's KV cache expands as it generates, and requests finish at different times.
  • Requests vary wildly: short chats, long documents, many users at once.

Good engines solve these with smarter memory management, batching, caching and optimised GPU kernels.

Key techniques inside modern engines

Continuous (in-flight) batching

Naive batching waits for a whole batch to finish before starting new requests, leaving the GPU idle as short requests complete. Continuous batching adds and removes requests at every decoding step, keeping the GPU full. It is the single biggest throughput improvement for multi-user serving.

PagedAttention

Introduced with vLLM in 2023, PagedAttention stores the KV cache in small fixed-size blocks, like virtual memory pages in an operating system, instead of one large contiguous buffer per request. This nearly eliminates wasted memory from fragmentation and over-reservation, so many more requests fit on a GPU at once. Most serious engines now use a paged KV cache.

Prefix caching

Many requests share the same beginning: a long system prompt, a document in a RAG pipeline, or earlier turns of a conversation. Prefix caching reuses the KV cache for that shared prefix instead of recomputing it, cutting time to first token dramatically. SGLang's RadixAttention organises cached prefixes in a tree for automatic reuse.

Optimised kernels

Fused attention kernels such as FlashAttention and FlashInfer, CUDA graphs, and hand-tuned matrix multiplications for FP8 and FP4 squeeze more from each GPU.

Quantization support

Engines differ in which formats they run fast: GGUF for llama.cpp, AWQ, GPTQ, FP8 and NVFP4 for GPU servers. See LLM quantization and NVFP4 explained.

Speculative decoding

Draft-and-verify methods speed up single-stream generation 2–3×. See speculative decoding explained.

Parallelism and disaggregation

Large models are split across GPUs with tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism; see distributed training and parallelism explained. Advanced deployments disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools, because the two phases stress hardware differently.

The engines compared

vLLM

Started at UC Berkeley, vLLM popularised PagedAttention and continuous batching and has become the most widely deployed open-source serving engine. It supports a very wide range of models, including mixture-of-experts and multimodal models, offers an OpenAI-compatible API, and runs on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and more. A good default for teams serving open models.

pip install vllm
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct --max-model-len 16384

SGLang

SGLang combines a fast runtime with RadixAttention prefix caching and strong support for structured output and multi-call programs, making it popular for agent workloads and large MoE models. It competes closely with vLLM on throughput, and the two projects borrow ideas from each other.

TensorRT-LLM

NVIDIA's library compiles models into optimised engines with the latest kernels, FP8 and NVFP4 support, in-flight batching and speculative decoding. It often achieves the highest throughput on NVIDIA data center GPUs such as the H100, H200 and B200, at the cost of more setup and less flexibility. It is often used together with NVIDIA's Triton Inference Server or Dynamo for deployment.

llama.cpp

A C/C++ engine that runs GGUF-quantized models on almost anything: laptops, desktops, Macs, Raspberry Pi-class boards and GPUs from every vendor. It can split models between GPU VRAM and system RAM, which lets you run models larger than your GPU memory, more slowly. It is the foundation of much of the local AI ecosystem.

Ollama and LM Studio

Both wrap llama.cpp-style inference in friendly tools. Ollama gives you a one-line command (ollama run llama3.1:8b) and a local API; LM Studio adds a graphical model browser and chat interface. Ideal for personal use, prototyping and private document chat. They are not designed for high-concurrency production serving. See how to run an LLM locally.

MLX

Apple's array framework for its own chips. mlx-lm runs and fine-tunes models efficiently on M-series Macs, taking advantage of large unified memory.

Throughput vs latency

You can explore how batch size, context and hardware affect speed in our LLM inference simulator.

Hardware sizing tips

  • VRAM sets the limit: weights plus KV cache for all concurrent requests must fit. See how much VRAM you need.
  • Bandwidth sets single-user speed: see GPU memory bandwidth.
  • Compute sets batched throughput: more tensor core TFLOPS lets you serve more users per GPU.
  • Rent before you buy: benchmark your workload on cloud GPUs first; compare prices in our GPU cloud price tracker.

How to choose

1. Just want to chat with models on your PC or Mac? Ollama or LM Studio. 2. Building a local app or running on unusual hardware? llama.cpp. 3. On a Mac and want speed? MLX or LM Studio's MLX backend. 4. Serving an open model to users from GPU servers? Start with vLLM or SGLang. 5. Need every last token per second on NVIDIA hardware? Evaluate TensorRT-LLM. 6. Always benchmark with your own prompts, context lengths and concurrency.

Frequently asked questions

Is Ollama good for production?

Ollama is excellent for local and small internal use, but engines built for high concurrency, such as vLLM and SGLang, achieve much higher throughput for many simultaneous users.

Is vLLM faster than llama.cpp?

On GPU servers with many concurrent requests, vLLM is usually much faster thanks to continuous batching and paged KV cache. For a single user on a laptop or with CPU offloading, llama.cpp is often the better fit.

Do these engines change model quality?

The engine itself does not, but the quantization format and sampling settings you choose can. Compare outputs when switching formats.

Can I use the OpenAI API format with these engines?

Yes. vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp's server all offer OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so most apps can switch with a URL change.

TITLE: MFU Explained: Model FLOPs Utilization and Why GPUs Never Hit Peak TFLOPS
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: Why does a GPU rated at 989 TFLOPS deliver far less in real AI training? An in-depth guide to model FLOPs utilization (MFU), hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU) and memory bandwidth utilization (MBU): how to calculate them, typical values, what wastes GPU time and how to improve it.
KEY: Model FLOPs utilization (MFU) measures how much of a GPU's peak compute is spent on the model's useful maths: achieved model FLOPs per second ÷ theoretical peak FLOPs per second. Large-scale LLM training typically reaches about 35–50% MFU; Meta reported 38–43% for Llama 3 405B on H100s, and Google reported 46.2% for PaLM 540B on TPUs. content:
Short answer

Model FLOPs utilization (MFU) measures how much of a GPU's peak compute is spent on the model's useful maths: achieved model FLOPs per second ÷ theoretical peak FLOPs per second. Large-scale LLM training typically reaches about 35–50% MFU; Meta reported 38–43% for Llama 3 405B on H100s, and Google reported 46.2% for PaLM 540B on TPUs. The rest is lost to communication, memory traffic, pipeline bubbles, inefficient kernels and failures. For inference, the more useful metric is often memory bandwidth utilization (MBU), because decoding is limited by memory, not compute.

Why "GPU utilization" in nvidia-smi is misleading

The utilization percentage shown by nvidia-smi means "a kernel was running during the sampling period", not "the tensor cores were busy". A GPU can show 100% utilization while doing only a small fraction of its possible maths, for example while running memory-bound kernels or waiting inside communication kernels. That is why AI engineers use MFU.

How to calculate MFU for training

For a dense transformer with N parameters, training costs about 6 FLOPs per parameter per token (2 for the forward pass, 4 for the backward pass), plus attention FLOPs that grow with sequence length:

FLOPs per token ≈ 6N + 12 × layers × d_model × seq_len   (attention term)
MFU = (tokens per second × FLOPs per token) / (number of GPUs × peak FLOPs per GPU)

Worked example

You train an 8B model on 64 H100 GPUs and process 1.2 million tokens per second across the cluster, ignoring the attention term for simplicity:

  • Model FLOPs per second = 1.2 × 10⁶ × 6 × 8 × 10⁹ = 5.76 × 10¹⁶
  • Peak = 64 × 989 × 10¹² (dense BF16) = 6.33 × 10¹⁶
  • MFU ≈ 91%, which is unrealistically high, so either the throughput number or the peak assumption needs checking.

A realistic run might achieve 500,000 tokens per second on those 64 GPUs: 2.4 × 10¹⁶ ÷ 6.33 × 10¹⁶ ≈ 38% MFU.

Always use dense peak figures at the precision you actually train in. Spec sheets often quote sparse numbers that are twice as high; see structured sparsity explained and how to read a GPU spec sheet.

MFU vs HFU

  • MFU counts only the FLOPs the model mathematically requires.
  • HFU (hardware FLOPs utilization) counts all FLOPs the hardware actually performs, including extra work such as recomputing activations for activation checkpointing.

HFU is always at least as high as MFU. MFU is preferred for comparing systems because it cannot be inflated by doing redundant work.

Typical MFU values

Where the missing FLOPs go

1. Communication: waiting for gradient all-reduces, weight all-gathers in FSDP, tensor-parallel exchanges and MoE all-to-all traffic. See distributed training and parallelism and InfiniBand vs Ethernet for AI. 2. Memory-bound operations: layer norm, softmax, activation functions, optimizer steps and data movement do little maths per byte. See the roofline model simulator. 3. Pipeline bubbles: stages waiting for micro-batches. 4. Small matrix shapes: matrices that do not fill the GPU's tensor core tiles waste capacity. 5. Kernel launch and Python overhead: many small operations instead of fused kernels. 6. Data loading and checkpointing: GPUs waiting for input or saving state. 7. Failures and restarts: at tens of thousands of GPUs, hardware faults are frequent; time lost to restarts lowers effective utilization over a whole run. 8. Power and thermal limits: GPUs may run below boost clocks under sustained load.

How to improve MFU

  • Use fused, optimised kernels: FlashAttention, fused optimizers, torch.compile, and well-tuned GEMM libraries.
  • Overlap communication with computation: start sending gradients for finished layers while others are still computing.
  • Pick good parallelism layouts: keep tensor parallelism inside NVLink domains; use enough micro-batches to shrink pipeline bubbles.
  • Use larger batches and sequence lengths where the training recipe allows, so matrices fill the hardware.
  • Choose hardware-friendly dimensions: hidden sizes and head dimensions that are multiples of 64 or 128.
  • Lower precision: mixed precision and FP8 raise absolute throughput even if MFU against the higher FP8 peak looks lower.
  • Fast data pipelines and asynchronous checkpointing.
  • Monitor with profilers: Nsight Systems, PyTorch Profiler and per-step tokens-per-second logs.

MBU: the inference metric

When generating tokens one at a time, each step reads all model weights (and the KV cache) from memory. The limit is bandwidth, so the useful metric is:

MBU = (bytes read per token × tokens per second) / peak memory bandwidth

Example: a 7B model in FP16 (14 GB) generating 150 tokens per second on an H100 (3.35 TB/s): 14 GB × 150 ÷ 3,350 GB/s ≈ 63% MBU. Good inference engines reach 60–80% MBU at small batch sizes. Batching more users raises compute use and pushes serving towards the compute-bound regime, where MFU becomes relevant again. See prefill vs decode, LLM inference engines compared and our LLM inference simulator.

Why MFU matters for cost

Training cost scales with GPU-hours. Raising MFU from 30% to 45% cuts the GPU-hours for the same model by a third. At frontier scale that can be tens of millions of dollars. Use MFU together with rental prices from our GPU cloud price tracker and the formulas in LLM training cost to estimate real budgets:

GPU-hours ≈ 6 × N × tokens / (peak FLOPs per GPU × MFU × 3,600)

Frequently asked questions

What is a good MFU?

For large-scale LLM pre-training, 40% or more is considered strong; over 50% is excellent. Small or communication-heavy jobs often see less.

Why can't GPUs reach 100% MFU?

Real models include many operations that are not large matrix multiplications, data must move between memory and GPUs, and GPUs in a cluster must synchronise. Peak figures assume perfect conditions that never occur in full training runs.

Do newer GPUs have higher MFU?

Not necessarily. Compute has grown faster than memory bandwidth and networking, so keeping faster GPUs busy is harder. Software and system design often decide MFU more than the chip.

Is MFU used for inference?

For high-throughput batched serving, yes. For single-user generation, memory bandwidth utilization is more meaningful.

TITLE: MHA vs MQA vs GQA vs MLA: Attention Variants and How They Shrink the KV Cache
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
IMG: MHA vs MQA vs GQA vs MLA
EXCERPT: Multi-head, multi-query, grouped-query and multi-head latent attention compared. How each attention variant works, the KV cache memory it needs per token with worked examples, the quality trade-offs, and why GQA and MLA power models like Llama 3 and DeepSeek-V3.
KEY: Modern LLMs use different flavours of attention mainly to shrink the KV cache, the memory that grows with every token and limits context length and the number of users per GPU. Multi-head attention (MHA) gives every query head its own keys and values. Multi-query attention (MQA) shares one key/value head across all query heads. Grouped-query attention (GQA), used by Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen and most open models, shares each key/value head among a group of query heads. Multi-head latent attention (MLA), introduced by DeepSeek, compresses keys and values into a small latent vector. GQA cuts KV memory by 4–8× with little quality loss; MLA cuts it further.
content:
Short answer

Modern LLMs use different flavours of attention mainly to shrink the KV cache, the memory that grows with every token and limits context length and the number of users per GPU. Multi-head attention (MHA) gives every query head its own keys and values. Multi-query attention (MQA) shares one key/value head across all query heads. Grouped-query attention (GQA), used by Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen and most open models, shares each key/value head among a group of query heads. Multi-head latent attention (MLA), introduced by DeepSeek, compresses keys and values into a small latent vector. GQA cuts KV memory by 4–8× with little quality loss; MLA cuts it further.

Why attention design matters for hardware

In a transformer, each attention head computes queries (Q), keys (K) and values (V) for every token. During generation, the keys and values of all previous tokens are stored in the KV cache so they are not recomputed. Its size is:

KV bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head_dim × bytes per value

The KV cache often uses more VRAM than the model weights at long context or high concurrency. It also has to be read from memory at every decoding step, so a smaller cache means faster, cheaper generation, because decode is limited by memory bandwidth. Reducing the number of KV heads is the most direct lever.

Multi-head attention (MHA)

The original 2017 design: if a layer has 32 query heads, it also has 32 key heads and 32 value heads. Each head can attend to different patterns, which is good for quality, but the KV cache is as large as it can be.

Used by: GPT-2, GPT-3, the original Llama 1 and many earlier models.

Multi-query attention (MQA)

Proposed by Noam Shazeer in 2019: keep many query heads but use a single shared key head and value head for all of them.

  • KV cache shrinks by a factor equal to the number of heads (for example 32×).
  • Decoding gets much faster.
  • Quality can drop, and training can be less stable, because all heads must use the same keys and values.

Used by: PaLM and Falcon, among others.

Grouped-query attention (GQA)

GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) is the middle ground: divide query heads into groups, and give each group one shared key/value head. With 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, every 4 query heads share a KV pair.

  • KV cache shrinks by query heads ÷ KV heads (4× in this example).
  • Quality stays very close to MHA.
  • Existing MHA models can even be "uptrained" into GQA with a small amount of extra training.

Used by: Llama 2 70B, Llama 3 and 3.1, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and most current open-weight models.

Multi-head latent attention (MLA)

Introduced in DeepSeek-V2 (2024) and used in DeepSeek-V3 and R1. Instead of caching full keys and values, MLA projects them into a compressed latent vector per token and caches only that, reconstructing per-head keys and values when needed. Matrix tricks let the up-projection be absorbed into other weights, so inference stays efficient. A small separate component carries rotary position information, because RoPE does not combine directly with the compression.

  • DeepSeek reported that DeepSeek-V2 reduced KV cache size by 93.3% compared with its earlier 67B MHA model, while matching or improving quality.
  • The trade-off is extra compute and implementation complexity.

Worked example: KV cache per token (FP16)

For a model with 32 layers, head dimension 128 and 32 query heads, similar to Llama 3 8B:

MLA's cache depends on its latent size; in DeepSeek's design it is comparable to a GQA model with only a few KV heads, while keeping quality closer to full MHA.

That difference decides how many users or how much context fits on a GPU. On an 80 GB H100 with 16 GB of weights (8B in FP16), MHA leaves room for about one 128K-token conversation; GQA with 8 KV heads leaves room for about four.

Comparison table

Other ways to shrink attention memory

  • Sliding-window attention: some layers only look at the last few thousand tokens, used by Mistral 7B, Gemma and gpt-oss in some layers.
  • KV cache quantization: store K and V in FP8 or 4-bit, halving or quartering memory. See LLM quantization.
  • Paged KV cache and prefix sharing: avoid waste and reuse shared prompts. See LLM inference engines compared.
  • Cross-layer KV sharing: adjacent layers reuse the same KV cache in some research designs.
  • Linear and hybrid attention: models that mix attention with state-space or linear-attention layers to keep memory constant over long sequences.

Effect on compute and FlashAttention

GQA and MQA reduce memory traffic but not the number of query heads, so the attention FLOPs stay similar. Kernels like FlashAttention handle GQA natively by loading each KV head once and reusing it for its whole query group, which increases arithmetic intensity and moves decoding closer to the compute-bound region on the roofline. Explore the attention mechanism itself in our attention simulator.

Frequently asked questions

Why do most new models use GQA?

It delivers most of MQA's memory and speed benefit with almost no quality loss, and it is simple to implement and supported by every major inference engine.

Is MLA better than GQA?

DeepSeek's results suggest MLA can match or beat MHA quality with an even smaller cache, but it adds complexity and is less widely supported in tools. GQA remains the default for most labs.

How do I find a model's KV head count?

Check its config.json on Hugging Face for num_key_value_heads alongside num_attention_heads, num_hidden_layers and head_dim, then use the formula above or our VRAM guide.

Does GQA change how I run models locally?

It means you can use longer contexts with the same VRAM. Models with fewer KV heads let you raise the context setting in tools like Ollama further before running out of memory.

Sources and further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017)
  • Shazeer, Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (MQA, 2019)
  • Ainslie et al., GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (2023)
  • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model (MLA, 2024)

TITLE: RoPE Explained: Rotary Positional Embeddings and How LLMs Handle Long Context
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: Transformers have no built-in sense of word order, so they need positional encodings. An in-depth guide to sinusoidal, learned and ALiBi encodings and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE), why RoPE won, and how techniques like position interpolation, NTK scaling and YaRN extend context windows to 128K tokens and beyond.
KEY: Attention treats its input as an unordered set, so transformers need positional encodings to know that "dog bites man" differs from "man bites dog". Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE), used by Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek and most modern LLMs, encodes position by rotating query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position. The dot product between a query and a key then depends only on their relative distance. content:
Short answer

Attention treats its input as an unordered set, so transformers need positional encodings to know that "dog bites man" differs from "man bites dog". Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE), used by Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek and most modern LLMs, encodes position by rotating query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position. The dot product between a query and a key then depends only on their relative distance. RoPE's structure also makes it possible to extend context length after training with methods like position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN, which is how many models reach 128K tokens or more.

Why transformers need positional information

Self-attention compares every token with every other token using dot products between query and key vectors. Nothing in that calculation depends on where tokens sit in the sequence. Shuffle the words and, without positional information, each token would get the same attention scores. Positional encodings inject order. For a refresher on the architecture, see What is a transformer?.

Earlier approaches

How RoPE works

The intuition

Think of each pair of numbers in a query or key vector as a point on a 2D plane. RoPE rotates that point by an angle that grows with the token's position: position 1 rotates a little, position 100 rotates a lot.

When the model computes the dot product between a query at position m and a key at position n, the rotations combine so the result depends on the difference m − n. The model therefore sees relative distance naturally, without adding anything to the token embeddings.

Multiple frequencies

A head dimension of 128 gives 64 pairs. Each pair rotates at a different frequency:

θ_i = base^(-2i / d),  for i = 0 … d/2 - 1
angle for pair i at position m = m × θ_i
  • High-frequency pairs (small i) rotate quickly and capture fine, local word order.
  • Low-frequency pairs (large i) rotate slowly and capture long-range position.

The base (often written as rope_theta) controls the range of frequencies. The original RoPE used 10,000; Llama 3 raised it to 500,000 to better support long contexts. You can find it in any model's config.json.

Why RoPE became the standard

  • Encodes relative position, which generalises better than absolute positions.
  • Applied directly to Q and K inside attention, so it adds negligible compute and no parameters.
  • Works with efficient kernels such as FlashAttention and with the KV cache, since keys are rotated once when cached.
  • Supports context extension after training.

Extending context length with RoPE

A model trained on sequences of 8K tokens has never seen rotation angles for position 50,000. Feeding it longer sequences usually causes quality to collapse. Several techniques modify RoPE so longer sequences map onto angles the model understands:

Position interpolation (PI)

Proposed by Meta researchers in 2023: squeeze positions by dividing them by a scale factor. To go from 4K to 16K, positions are divided by 4 so every position falls inside the trained range. A short fine-tuning run adapts the model. Downside: high-frequency, local information gets compressed too.

NTK-aware scaling

Instead of scaling all frequencies equally, this approach increases the RoPE base, stretching low frequencies (long range) more than high frequencies (local detail). It works reasonably even without fine-tuning.

YaRN

YaRN (2023) combines frequency-dependent interpolation with an attention temperature adjustment, preserving local detail while extending range. It is widely used to extend open models to 128K tokens and is supported by inference engines such as vLLM and llama.cpp through rope_scaling settings.

Training with long context

The most reliable approach is to raise the RoPE base and continue pre-training on long documents. Llama 3.1, for example, was extended to a 128K-token context through a dedicated long-context training stage. Modern models may also mix layers with full attention and layers with sliding-window attention.

Long context is about more than positions

Even with good positional encoding, long context is limited by:

  • KV cache memory, which grows linearly with length; see MHA vs MQA vs GQA vs MLA.
  • Attention compute, which grows with the square of length during prefill.
  • Training memory, solved with context parallelism; see distributed training and parallelism.
  • Effective use of long inputs: models often use the middle of very long prompts less well. See What is a context window?.

A tiny RoPE implementation

import torch

def apply_rope(x, positions, base=10000.0):
    # x: (seq, heads, dim) with even dim
    d = x.shape[-1]
    inv_freq = base ** (-torch.arange(0, d, 2, dtype=torch.float32) / d)
    angles = positions[:, None].float() * inv_freq[None, :]   # (seq, d/2)
    cos, sin = angles.cos()[:, None, :], angles.sin()[:, None, :]
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2] = x1 * cos - x2 * sin
    out[..., 1::2] = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return out

Apply it to queries and keys (not values) before computing attention scores. Production implementations often pair dimensions differently (first half with second half) for speed, but the maths is equivalent.

Frequently asked questions

Does RoPE add parameters to the model?

No. The rotation angles are fixed by the formula; nothing is learned.

Why is it applied only to queries and keys?

Position needs to influence which tokens attend to which, which is decided by the query-key dot product. Values carry content and do not need rotation.

Can I extend a model's context myself?

Inference engines let you set rope_scaling (for example YaRN with a factor) to run beyond the trained length, but quality usually drops without long-context fine-tuning. Check the model card for supported settings.

What does a larger RoPE base do?

It slows the lowest-frequency rotations, so positions remain distinguishable over longer distances, which helps long-context training.

TITLE: AI Scaling Laws Explained: Kaplan, Chinchilla, Over-Training and Test-Time Compute
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: Scaling laws describe how AI models improve predictably as you add compute, data and parameters. An in-depth guide to the Kaplan and Chinchilla laws, compute-optimal training, why modern models are over-trained, test-time scaling with reasoning models, data limits, and what scaling means for GPU demand.

content:
Short answer

Scaling laws are empirical rules showing that a language model's loss falls smoothly and predictably as you increase training compute, model size and data. OpenAI's 2020 Kaplan laws favoured making models bigger; DeepMind's 2022 Chinchilla study showed models should be trained on about 20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal results. Today, labs deliberately over-train smaller models on far more data to make them cheaper to run, and a new axis, test-time compute, lets reasoning models improve by thinking longer. Scaling is the main reason AI labs keep buying ever larger GPU clusters.

What a scaling law is

Train many models of different sizes with different amounts of data and compute, plot their test loss on log-log axes, and the points fall on remarkably straight lines. That means loss follows a power law:

Loss(C) ≈ L_min + (C_0 / C)^α

where C is training compute and α is a small exponent. The practical meaning: every time you multiply compute by a fixed factor, loss drops by a predictable amount, with diminishing returns. Labs use these curves to predict how a huge model will perform before spending months training it, by extrapolating from small experiments.

The training compute itself is approximately:

C ≈ 6 × N × D   (FLOPs; N = parameters, D = training tokens)

See AI training vs inference for where the 6 comes from.

The Kaplan scaling laws (OpenAI, 2020)

Kaplan et al. found that loss scales as a power law with model size, dataset size and compute, over many orders of magnitude, and that architecture details (depth vs width) matter much less than scale. Their analysis suggested that, for a fixed compute budget, it is best to grow model size faster than data, training very large models on relatively few tokens and stopping early.

That guided the era of GPT-3 (175B parameters trained on about 300 billion tokens, under 2 tokens per parameter) and other giant models.

The Chinchilla scaling laws (DeepMind, 2022)

Hoffmann et al. re-ran the analysis with better methodology, training over 400 models, and reached a different conclusion: parameters and data should grow roughly equally with compute. The compute-optimal ratio is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

They proved it with Chinchilla: a 70B-parameter model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens, using the same compute as their 280B-parameter Gopher. Chinchilla outperformed Gopher, GPT-3 and other larger models on most benchmarks, while being four times smaller and cheaper to run.

Why modern models are "over-trained"

Chinchilla optimises training compute only. But a popular model is then used billions of times, and inference cost depends on model size. A smaller model trained far beyond the Chinchilla ratio costs more to train than strictly necessary but is much cheaper to serve, and it keeps improving with more data.

That is why Meta trained Llama 3 8B on about 15 trillion tokens, nearly 100 times the Chinchilla-optimal amount, and why small language models have become so capable. Inference-aware scaling laws formalise this trade-off by adding expected lifetime inference to the cost.

Test-time compute: the second scaling axis

Since 2024, reasoning models have shown a new kind of scaling: performance on hard problems improves as the model spends more compute at inference time, generating longer chains of thought or sampling multiple solutions and choosing the best. OpenAI reported that o1's accuracy rose steadily with both more reinforcement-learning training compute and more thinking time.

This changes hardware economics. Instead of compute being concentrated in one training run, a large share shifts to serving: every hard question can consume thousands of extra tokens. See how much energy AI uses and speculative decoding for how the industry is trying to make that cheaper.

Other scaling dimensions

  • Reinforcement learning compute: training reasoning models with large-scale RL has its own scaling behaviour. See What is reinforcement learning?.
  • Mixture of experts: MoE models shift the curves, giving lower loss for the same compute by adding parameters that are not all used per token. See mixture of experts.
  • Data quality: better-filtered and synthetic data can beat raw quantity, effectively moving the curve down.
  • Precision: recent research studies how low-precision training (FP8, FP4) interacts with scaling.

Limits and open questions

  • Data: high-quality public text is finite. Epoch AI estimates that the stock of human-generated public text could be fully used by frontier training runs around the late 2020s, pushing labs towards synthetic data, multimodal data and more efficient learning.
  • Loss vs abilities: smooth loss curves do not always translate into smooth gains on specific tasks. Some abilities seem to "emerge" suddenly, though researchers argue this is partly an artefact of how benchmarks are scored. See AI benchmarks explained.
  • Diminishing returns: power laws mean each improvement costs more compute than the last.
  • Energy and hardware: the largest training runs now need power on the scale of large industrial facilities and chip supply constrained by advanced packaging.
  • Does scaling lead to AGI? This is the central debate in AI. See What is AGI?, When will AGI arrive? and the intelligence explosion.

What scaling laws mean for GPU demand

Training compute for frontier models has grown by roughly four to five times per year over the past decade, according to Epoch AI. Combined with test-time scaling and billions of daily users, this drives demand for GPU clusters, AI data centers and new chips such as NVIDIA Rubin. You can estimate any model's training compute and cost with the formulas in LLM training cost, and follow rental prices in our GPU cloud price tracker.

Quick estimate: how many GPU-hours for a Chinchilla-optimal 70B model?

  • Tokens: 20 × 70B = 1.4T
  • Compute: 6 × 70 × 10⁹ × 1.4 × 10¹² ≈ 5.9 × 10²³ FLOPs
  • H100 at 989 dense BF16 TFLOPS and 40% MFU: about 396 TFLOPS effective
  • GPU-hours ≈ 5.9 × 10²³ ÷ (3.96 × 10¹⁴ × 3,600) ≈ 413,000 H100-hours

Frequently asked questions

What is the Chinchilla ratio?

About 20 training tokens per model parameter, the amount that minimises loss for a fixed training compute budget according to DeepMind's 2022 study.

Are scaling laws still valid?

The core finding that loss improves predictably with compute has held across many orders of magnitude. What has changed is how labs spend compute: more data per parameter, more reinforcement learning and more inference-time reasoning.

Why don't labs just train much bigger models?

Bigger models cost more to train and much more to serve, data is limited, and over-trained smaller models often give a better balance of quality and cost.

Do scaling laws apply to images and video?

Yes. Similar power laws have been found for vision, speech, video and multimodal models, as well as for diffusion models.

TITLE: Speculative Decoding Explained: How LLMs Generate Text 2–3× Faster Without Losing Quality
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by letting a small draft model guess several tokens ahead and having the big model verify them in one pass. How it works, why it is lossless, acceptance rates, draft models vs Medusa, EAGLE and multi-token prediction, and when it helps on real GPUs.
KEY: Speculative decoding makes large language models generate text faster by splitting the work in two: a cheap draft model quickly proposes the next several tokens, and the large target model checks all of them in a single forward pass, keeping every token it agrees with. Because the big model's verification step is mathematically exact, the output has the same quality and distribution as normal decoding, typically with 2–3× faster token generation for a single user. It works because decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, leaving GPU compute idle that verification can use for free.
content:
Short answer

Speculative decoding makes large language models generate text faster by splitting the work in two: a cheap draft model quickly proposes the next several tokens, and the large target model checks all of them in a single forward pass, keeping every token it agrees with. Because the big model's verification step is mathematically exact, the output has the same quality and distribution as normal decoding, typically with 2–3× faster token generation for a single user. It works because decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, leaving GPU compute idle that verification can use for free.

The problem: decoding wastes the GPU

When a large language model generates text, it produces one token at a time. Each step requires reading essentially all of the model's weights from GPU memory. For a 70B-parameter model in FP16, that is about 140 GB of reads to produce a single token.

Modern GPUs can do far more arithmetic than their memory can feed. An H100 offers about 989 dense BF16 TFLOPS but "only" about 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth. In the decode phase, a single sequence uses roughly 2 FLOPs per byte of weights read, so the tensor cores sit mostly idle. You can see this on the roofline model simulator: batch-1 decoding sits far to the left, deep in the memory-bound region.

Key insight: checking k tokens costs almost the same as generating one, because the weights are read once either way. Speculative decoding exploits this.

How speculative decoding works

1. Draft: a small, fast model (or a cheap extra head) generates k candidate tokens, for example 4 to 8, one after another. 2. Verify: the large target model runs one forward pass over the prompt plus all k draft tokens, producing its own probability distribution at every position, just like prefill. 3. Accept or reject: going left to right, each draft token is accepted with a probability based on how much the target model agrees with it. At the first rejection, the target model's corrected token is used instead, and the rest of the draft is discarded. 4. Bonus token: if all k drafts are accepted, the target model's prediction for position k+1 is added for free. 5. Repeat from the new position.

Each verification step therefore produces between 1 and k+1 tokens for roughly the cost of one large-model step.

Why it is lossless

The acceptance rule from the original papers (Leviathan et al. at Google and Chen et al. at DeepMind, 2022–2023) is a form of rejection sampling:

accept draft token x with probability min(1, p_target(x) / p_draft(x))
if rejected: sample from normalize(max(0, p_target - p_draft))

This guarantees that the final tokens follow exactly the target model's distribution, at any temperature. With greedy decoding (temperature 0), the rule simplifies to "accept if the target model's top token matches". Unlike quantization or distillation, speculative decoding never changes what the model would say, only how fast it says it.

How much faster? The maths

Let α be the average probability that a draft token is accepted and k the draft length. The expected number of tokens produced per verification step is:

E[tokens per step] = (1 - α^(k+1)) / (1 - α)

Real speed-up is lower than these numbers because drafting and verification have overhead. In practice, 2–3× end-to-end speed-ups are common for chat and coding, and more for highly predictable text such as code edits, structured output or summaries that copy from the input.

What drives acceptance:

  • Draft quality: a draft model from the same family, with the same tokenizer, agrees far more often.
  • Task predictability: boilerplate code and JSON are easier to guess than creative writing.
  • Temperature: higher temperatures reduce agreement. See LLM temperature explained.

Types of drafters

When speculative decoding helps, and when it does not

Helps most:

  • Single-user or low-batch serving, where decode is heavily memory-bound
  • Local inference on consumer GPUs and Macs; see how to run an LLM locally
  • Long outputs: code generation, long answers and reasoning models that produce thousands of thinking tokens
  • Latency-sensitive applications such as coding assistants and voice agents

Helps less:

  • High-batch serving: with many concurrent users, the GPU is already busy computing, so spare FLOPs shrink. Gains fall and can turn negative at very large batch sizes.
  • Low acceptance: a poorly matched draft wastes compute.
  • Tight memory: a separate draft model needs extra VRAM and its own KV cache.

Hardware and memory considerations

  • Extra VRAM: a 1B draft model adds about 2 GB in FP16 plus its KV cache. Head-based methods (Medusa, EAGLE) add much less.
  • Compute headroom: GPUs with high FLOPs-to-bandwidth ratios, such as the H100, B200 and RTX 5090, have the most idle compute to spend on verification.
  • Mixture-of-experts models: verification of several tokens may activate more experts, reducing the free-compute advantage somewhat. See mixture of experts.
  • Attention cost: verifying k tokens adds k positions of attention, which grows with context length; FlashAttention keeps this efficient.

Using speculative decoding today

  • vLLM and SGLang: support draft models, EAGLE-style heads, MTP and n-gram speculation through configuration options. See LLM inference engines compared.
  • TensorRT-LLM: supports draft-target, Medusa, EAGLE and lookahead decoding on NVIDIA GPUs.
  • llama.cpp: supports a draft model with the same vocabulary, useful for local setups.
  • Hosted APIs: many providers already use speculative decoding behind the scenes; it is one reason some APIs are much faster than a naive deployment of the same model.

A typical local setup: run a 70B target with a 1B–3B draft from the same family, set draft length to 4–8, and measure tokens per second with and without it on your own prompts.

Frequently asked questions

Does speculative decoding reduce output quality?

No. With the standard acceptance rule, outputs follow exactly the same probability distribution as the target model alone. Only speed changes.

Why not just use the small model?

The small model is faster but less capable. Speculative decoding gives you the large model's quality at closer to the small model's speed.

What is a good draft length?

Usually 3 to 8 tokens. Longer drafts help when acceptance is high but waste compute when it is low. Many engines tune this automatically.

Does it reduce cost per token?

For low-batch, latency-focused serving, yes, because each GPU-second produces more tokens. For high-throughput batch serving, the benefit is smaller because the GPU is already compute-busy.
